```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(ggnewscale)

data_dir <- "datasets"

read_singstat_wide <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE)

  header_index <- which(
    stringr::str_detect(lines, "^Data\\s*Series\\s*,")
  )[1]

  if (is.na(header_index)) {
    stop("No 'Data Series' header found in: ", path)
  }

  raw <- readr::read_csv(
    path,
    skip = header_index - 1,
    na = c("", "na", "NA", "N.A.", "-"),
    show_col_types = FALSE
  )

  raw <- dplyr::rename_with(raw, trimws)
  names(raw)[1] <- "data_series"

  raw |>
    mutate(data_series = stringr::str_squish(data_series)) |>
    filter(!is.na(data_series), data_series != "")
}

to_long_years <- function(data) {
  data |>
    mutate(across(matches("^\\d{4}$"), as.character)) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = matches("^\\d{4}$"),
      names_to = "year",
      values_to = "value"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      year = as.integer(year),
      value = readr::parse_number(as.character(value))
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(year))
}

standardise_age_group <- function(x) {
  x |>
    stringr::str_squish() |>
    stringr::str_replace_all("\\s*-\\s*", "-")
}

age_groups <- c(
  "15-19 Years",
  "20-24 Years",
  "25-29 Years",
  "30-34 Years",
  "35-39 Years",
  "40-44 Years",
  "45-49 Years"
)

age_group_colours <- c(
  "15-19 Years" = "#D73027",
  "20-24 Years" = "#FC8D59",
  "25-29 Years" = "#FEE08B",
  "30-34 Years" = "#91CF60",
  "35-39 Years" = "#1A9850",
  "40-44 Years" = "#4575B4",
  "45-49 Years" = "#7B3294"
)

fertility_wide <- read_singstat_wide(file.path(data_dir, "BirthsAndFertilityRatesAnnual.csv"))
lfpr_wide <- read_singstat_wide(file.path(data_dir, "M182201.csv"))

asfr_by_age <- fertility_wide |>
  mutate(age_group = standardise_age_group(data_series)) |>
  filter(age_group %in% age_groups) |>
  to_long_years() |>
  transmute(
    year,
    age_group = factor(age_group, levels = age_groups),
    asfr = value
  ) |>
  filter(year >= 1980, !is.na(asfr)) |>
  arrange(age_group, year)

tfr_annual <- fertility_wide |>
  filter(data_series == "Total Fertility Rate (TFR)") |>
  to_long_years() |>
  transmute(year, tfr = value)

lfpr_female <- lfpr_wide |>
  mutate(
    section = case_when(
      data_series == "Female Resident Participation Rate" ~ "Female",
      data_series %in% c(
        "Total Resident Participation Rate",
        "Male Resident Participation Rate"
      ) ~ "Other",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  tidyr::fill(section, .direction = "down") |>
  filter(section == "Female", data_series != "Female Resident Participation Rate") |>
  mutate(age_group = standardise_age_group(data_series)) |>
  filter(age_group %in% age_groups) |>
  to_long_years() |>
  transmute(
    year,
    age_group = factor(age_group, levels = age_groups),
    female_lfpr_pct = value
  ) |>
  filter(year >= 1990, !is.na(female_lfpr_pct)) |>
  arrange(age_group, year)

recession_events <- tibble(
  recession = c(
    "1985 recession",
    "Asian Financial Crisis",
    "Global Financial Crisis",
    "COVID-19 recession"
  ),
  year = c(1985, 1998, 2009, 2020)
) |>
  mutate(xmin = year - 0.55, xmax = year + 0.55)

birth_policy_events <- tibble(
  year = c(1984, 1987, 2001, 2004, 2008, 2013),
  policy = c(
    "Graduate Mothers Scheme",
    "Have Three or More policy",
    "Baby Bonus",
    "M&P Package",
    "Enhanced M&P Package",
    "Enhanced M&P Package"
  ),
  label_level = c(1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2)
)

asfr_total_by_year <- asfr_by_age |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(total_asfr = sum(asfr, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

lfpr_scale <- max(asfr_total_by_year$total_asfr, na.rm = TRUE) / 100

lfpr_line <- lfpr_female |>
  filter(year >= min(asfr_by_age$year), year <= max(asfr_by_age$year))

    inherit.aes = FALSE,

    data = recession_events,
    aes(x = year, y = Inf, label = recession),

    size = 3.2,
    fontface = "bold",

  ) +

    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    linetype = "dotted",
    linewidth = 0.75,
    colour = "black"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = birth_policy_events,

      x = year,
      y = Inf,

    ),

    size = 3,

  ) +
  geom_col(
    data = asfr_by_age,

    width = 0.82,

  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = lfpr_line,
    aes(x = year, y = female_lfpr_pct * lfpr_scale, group = age_group),
    colour = "ghostwhite",
    linewidth = 2.1,
    lineend = "round"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = lfpr_line,
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = female_lfpr_pct * lfpr_scale,
      colour = age_group,
      group = age_group
    ),
    linewidth = 1.15,
    linetype = "dashed",
    alpha = 0.98,
    lineend = "round"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(1980, 2025.6),
    breaks = seq(1980, 2025, 5),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.005, 0.005))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "ASFR (births per 1,000 women)",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(
      ~ . / lfpr_scale,
      name = "Female LFPR (%)",
      breaks = seq(0, 100, 20)
    ),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.40))
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = age_group_colours,
    name = "Age group",
    labels = function(x) str_remove(x, " Years")
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = age_group_colours,
    name = "Age group",
    labels = function(x) str_remove(x, " Years")
  ) +
  guides(
    fill = guide_legend(title = "Age group", order = 1, nrow = 1),
    colour = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Singapore fertility and female labour-force participation by age group",
    subtitle = "Stacked bars show ASFR by age group. Dashed lines show female LFPR. Shaded bands mark recessions; dotted lines mark major policies.",
    x = "Year",
    caption = "Associations shown, not causation."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9.5),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 7.5, colour = "grey40"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.box = "horizontal",
    plot.margin = margin(0, 8, 6, 8)
  )

  left_join(lfpr_aggregate, by = "year") |>

age_band_stops <- tibble(
  midpoint = c(17, 22, 27, 32, 37, 42, 47),
  colour = c("#D73027", "#FC8D59", "#FEE08B", "#A6D96A", "#1A9850", "#4575B4", "#762A83")
)

age_colour_ramp <- colorRamp(age_band_stops$colour, space = "Lab")

birth_age_to_colour <- function(age) {
  t <- approx(
    age_band_stops$midpoint,
    seq(0, 1, length.out = nrow(age_band_stops)),
    xout = age,
    rule = 2
  )$y
  cols <- age_colour_ramp(t)
  rgb(cols[, 1], cols[, 2], cols[, 3], maxColorValue = 255)
}

insight1_legend_colours <- birth_age_to_colour(insight1_legend_ages)

insight1_data <- insight1_data |>

family_size_wide <- read_singstat_wide(file.path(data_dir, "ResidentEverMarriedFemalesByAgeGroupAndNumberOfChildrenBornAnnual.csv"))
cpi_wide <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "ConsumerPriceIndexCPI2024AsBaseYearMonthly.csv"),
  na = c("", "na", "NA", "N.A.", "-"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  rename(data_series = DataSeries)

cpi_annual <- cpi_wide |>
  filter(data_series == "All Items") |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = matches("^\\d{4}[A-Za-z]{3}$"),
    names_to = "period",
    values_to = "cpi_index"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(str_sub(period, 1, 4)),
    cpi_index = readr::parse_number(as.character(cpi_index))
  ) |>
  filter(year >= 1990, year <= 2025) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(cpi_index = mean(cpi_index, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

family_size_tagged <- family_size_wide |>
  mutate(
    age_group = if_else(str_detect(data_series, "^\\d+\\s*-\\s*\\d+\\s+Years$"), data_series, NA_character_),
    children_born = case_when(
      data_series == "None" ~ "None",
      data_series == "1 Child" ~ "1 child",
      data_series == "2 Children" ~ "2 children",
      data_series %in% c("3 Children", "4 Or More Children", "3 Or More Children") ~ "3 or more children",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  tidyr::fill(age_group, .direction = "down")

family_size_40_49 <- family_size_tagged |>
  filter(str_detect(age_group, "^40\\s*-\\s*49"), !is.na(children_born)) |>
  to_long_years() |>
  transmute(year, children_born, females = value) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(
    total_females = sum(females, na.rm = TRUE),
    share_pct = females / total_females * 100
  ) |>
  ungroup()

family_size_selected <- family_size_40_49 |>
  filter(year %in% c(1990, 2000, 2010, 2020, 2025)) |>
  group_by(year, children_born) |>
  summarise(share_pct = sum(share_pct, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    children_born = factor(
      children_born,
      levels = c("3 or more children", "2 children", "1 child", "None")
    ),
    label = if_else(share_pct >= 7, paste0(round(share_pct, 0), "%"), "")
  )

cpi_selected <- cpi_annual |>
  filter(year %in% c(1990, 2000, 2010, 2020, 2025)) |>
  arrange(year) |>
  mutate(
    cost_step_pct = (cpi_index / lag(cpi_index) - 1) * 100,
    cost_fill_pct = replace_na(cost_step_pct, 0),
    cost_label = if_else(
      year == 1990,
      "Cost baseline",
      paste0("+", round(cost_step_pct), "% cost")
    )
  )

    title = "Did completed family size shift smaller?",
    subtitle = "Selected years. Top strip shows CPI increase from the previous selected year.",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Share of women aged 40 to 49",
    caption = "Cost labels compare each selected year with the previous selected year. Family-size bars remain percentages."
  ) +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.box = "vertical",
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

)

  1985, "1985", "Severe", 6,
  1998, "1998", "Severe", 6,
  2001, "2001", "Moderate", 5,
  2009, "2009", "Most severe", 6,
  2020, "2020", "Most severe", 4
)

policy_window <- policy_events |>
  crossing(relative_year = -5:10) |>
  mutate(year = event_year + relative_year) |>
  left_join(tfr_annual, by = "year") |>
  mutate(
    event_label = factor(
      event_label,
      levels = c("Stop at Two", "Have Three or More", "Baby Bonus", "Marriage and Parenthood package")
    )
  )

shock_window <- policy_events |>
  crossing(economic_shocks) |>
  mutate(
    relative_year = shock_year - event_year,
    recovery_years = quarters_below_peak / 4,
    relative_recovery_end = relative_year + recovery_years,
    event_label = factor(
      event_label,
      levels = c("Stop at Two", "Have Three or More", "Baby Bonus", "Marriage and Parenthood package")
    )
  ) |>
  filter(relative_year <= 10, relative_recovery_end >= -5) |>
  mutate(
    xmin = pmax(relative_year, -5),
    xmax = pmin(relative_recovery_end, 10)
  )

# Concise validation checks for the plot-ready tables
family_share_check <- family_size_40_49 |>
  summarise(total_share = sum(share_pct), .by = year)

stopifnot(
  all(c(1980, 2025) %in% asfr_by_age$year),
  all(c(1990, 2025) %in% lfpr_female$year),
  setequal(as.character(unique(asfr_by_age$age_group)), age_groups),
  nrow(distinct(asfr_by_age, year, age_group)) == nrow(asfr_by_age),
  nrow(distinct(lfpr_female, year, age_group)) == nrow(lfpr_female),
  all(between(lfpr_female$female_lfpr_pct, 0, 100)),
  all(abs(family_share_check$total_share - 100) < 0.01),
  !anyNA(cpi_selected$cpi_index),
  !anyNA(policy_window$tfr)
)

p_insight4 <- ggplot(policy_window, aes(x = relative_year, y = tfr, colour = policy_stance)) +
  geom_rect(
    data = shock_window,
    aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = severity),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    alpha = 0.24
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey35") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.3) +
  geom_label(
    data = shock_window,
    aes(x = (xmin + xmax) / 2, y = Inf, label = shock_label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    vjust = 1.2,
    size = 2.8,
    label.size = 0.15,
    fill = "white",
    colour = "grey35"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ event_label, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Anti-natalist" = "#D95F02", "Pro-natalist" = "#1B9E77")) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    limits = c("Moderate", "Severe", "Most severe"),
    values = c(
      "Most severe" = "#B2182B",
      "Severe" = "#8073AC",
      "Moderate" = "#D8DAEB"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-5, 0, 5, 10)) +
  labs(
    title = "Did recessions and policies explain fertility changes?",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = policy year. Shaded bands show economic recovery duration and recession severity.",
    x = "Years from policy",
    y = "TFR",
    colour = "Policy stance",
    fill = "Economic shock severity",
    caption = "Policy and recession markers provide context only. Timing is not causal proof."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

## Framing the Question {.story-slide}

::: kicker
Research focus
:::

::: hr-accent
:::

::: {.story-question .fragment style="font-size:30px;"}
<strong>Why this matters</strong>

- Below replacement level → population cannot sustain itself naturally

- Citizen population will shrink → impacts future sustainability

- Hard to reverse → fewer women of childbearing age over time
:::

::: {.story-question .fragment style="font-size:24px;"}
We explore how Singapore's fertility decline has occurred alongside
changes in family formation, education, labour-force participation,
policies and economic conditions.
:::

## The Original CNA Visualisation {.clean-slide}

::::::: two-col

Source: CNA birth-count visualisation on Singapore citizen births.

::::

:::: side-note
::: kicker
Original story
:::

##### Annual citizen births fell over the past decade

The chart shows the decline in Singapore's birth rate from 2012 to 2022.

**2 Primary Dimensions:**

- **Year** — Annual observations on the x-axis.
- **Number of Singapore Citizen Births** — Birth counts represented by
  bar height.

**Supporting design elements:**

- **Period grouping** — Colour shades compare 2013–2017 and 2018–2022.
- **Average birth annotations** — Five-year averages show changes
  between periods.
- **Direct value labels** — Exact values above bars improve readability.
::::
:::::::

## From birth counts to fertility behaviour {.clean-slide}

::: kicker
Redesign logic
:::

::: hr-accent
:::

<h3 style="margin-top: 1em;">

Each improvement addresses a weakness in the original chart

</h3>

::::::::: card-grid-3
:::: {.info-card .blue .fragment .fade-up fragment-index="1"}
::: num
01
:::

<h3>Better fertility measurement</h3>

<p>Replace raw birth counts with age-specific fertility rates to show
how fertility patterns differ across maternal age groups.</p>
::::

:::: {.info-card .blue .fragment .fade-up fragment-index="1"}
::: num
02
:::

<h3>Extended Historical view & context</h3>

<p>Extend the annual timeline and incorporate female LFPR, policy
milestones and recession periods to provide wider demographic and
economic context.</p>
::::

:::: {.info-card .blue .fragment .fade-up fragment-index="1"}
::: num
03
:::

<h3>Clearer visual communication</h3>

<p>Use consistent age-group colours, explicit axes, legends and
annotation styles to make the visualisation easier to interpret
independently.</p>
::::
:::::::::

::: {.story-question .fragment fragment-index="2"}
The improvement is not to add more variables for the sake of it. The
goal is to make the main fertility story more explainable and
self-contained.

## Raw Layouts and Cleaning Needs {.clean-slide}

::: kicker
Data engineering detail
:::

::: hr-accent
:::

<h4>The raw files did not all arrive in analysis-ready form</h4>

::::::::::::::::::: engineering-card-grid
:::: {.engineering-card .stat-pop}
::: eng-num
01
:::

<h3>Metadata rows</h3>

<p><strong>Fix:</strong> detect the true <code>Data Series</code> header
before reading.</p>

Prevents metadata from becoming fake observations.
::::

:::: {.engineering-card .stat-pop}
::: eng-num
02
:::

<h3>Wide year columns</h3>

<p><strong>Fix:</strong> pivot years into long format.</p>

Allows filtering, joining and plotting by year.
::::

:::: {.engineering-card .stat-pop}
::: eng-num
03
:::

<h3>Inconsistent labels</h3>

<p><strong>Fix:</strong> standardise age groups such as <code>20-24
Years</code>.</p>

Ensures ASFR and LFPR age bands match.
::::

:::: {.engineering-card .stat-pop}
::: eng-num
04
:::

<h3>Mixed value types</h3>

<p><strong>Fix:</strong> parse numeric values after reshaping.</p>

Prevents text values from breaking calculations.
::::

:::: {.engineering-card .stat-pop}
::: eng-num
05
:::

<h3>Different ranges</h3>

<p><strong>Fix:</strong> keep available years and show honest gaps.</p>

Avoids inventing observations for missing periods.
::::

:::: {.engineering-card .stat-pop}
::: eng-num
06
:::

<h3>Event context</h3>

<p><strong>Fix:</strong> create manual policy and recession event
tables.</p>

Keeps annotations reproducible and separate from measured data.
::::

:::: {.engineering-card .stat-pop}
::: eng-num
07
:::

<h3>Different units</h3>

<p><strong>Fix:</strong> keep ASFR, TFR, LFPR, ages and percentages
clearly separated.</p>

Avoids misleading comparisons across incompatible measures.
::::

:::: {.engineering-card .stat-pop}
::: eng-num
08
:::

<h3>Derived measures</h3>

<p><strong>Fix:</strong> compute shares, policy-relative years and
visual encodings.</p>

Turns raw data into story-ready variables.

## Insights & Analysis {#insights-analysis .section-divider background-image="images/insightsanalysis-bg.jpg" background-size="cover" background-position="center" background-opacity="0.5" transition="slide"}

::: section-number
07
:::

::: divider-title
Insights & Analysis
:::

::: divider-subtitle
Four supporting insights answer what changed underneath the fertility
decline.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Insight 1: Education, LFPR and Birth Timing {.clean-slide}

::::: {.two-col .plot-wide}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.8
#| fig-height: 5.2
p_insight1
```

:::: side-note
::: kicker
Insight 1
:::

<h3>What is driving the increase in female LFPR?</h3>

<p>Female LFPR increased from approximately 50% in 1990 to 60% in
2025.</p>

<p>Over the same period, the number of female university graduates
increased substantially.</p>

<p>The median age at first birth also rose from approximately 28 years
in 1990 to 32 years in 2025.</p>

<p><strong>Interpretation:</strong> Female LFPR rose alongside
increasing educational attainment. As more women pursued higher
education and established careers, first birth and family formation also
shifted later \[11\].</p>

<p><strong>Research support:</strong> A peer-reviewed study published in
the Journal of Social Policy associates delayed family formation and
parenthood in Singapore with educational expansion, increased female
labour-market participation, and changing attitudes towards marriage and
childbearing. This is consistent with the parallel movement observed in
our data, although it does not establish direct causation. \[11\]</p>
::::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Insight 2: Longer Schooling and Younger-Age Fertility {.clean-slide}

::::: {.two-col .plot-wide}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.8
#| fig-height: 5.2
p_insight2
```

:::: side-note
::: kicker
Insight 2
:::

<h3>Women's literacy rates in Singapore</h3>

<p>Government policies drove female literacy rates up. 1961: Free
primary education was offered. 1994: School curriculum was unified for
all sexes. 2003: Quota for female intake to NUS medical school
lifted.</p>

<p>With more equal opportunities, women are now spending more time in
school, pursuing higher levels of education.</p>

<p>Therefore, female LFPR for women aged 15-19 and 20-24 has dropped
because young women at those ages are still schooling and hence, not
able to join the workforce.</p>

<p><strong>Interpretation:</strong> Education once went to sons; women
were confined to labour or homemaking. Women now pursue higher education
and delay starting a family, extending the same pattern of later labour
force entry seen across this period.</p>

<p><strong>Research support:</strong> Research published in the Journal
of Social Policy and the Journal of Population Research notes that
longer participation in education may postpone subsequent transitions
into employment, marriage and parenthood. This supports our
interpretation that extended schooling forms part of a wider delay in
adult and family formation. \[11\]\[12\]</p>
::::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Insight 3: Completed Family Size Became Smaller {.clean-slide}

::::: {.two-col .plot-wide}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.2
#| fig-height: 5.5
p_insight3b
```

:::: side-note
::: kicker
Insight 3
:::

<h3>Later family formation connects to smaller completed families</h3>

<p>Among ever-married women aged 40 to 49, larger families became less
common.</p>

<p>Smaller family-size categories became more prominent over time.</p>

<p>Rising consumer price index over the years shows the increasing cost
of living.</p>

<p><strong>Interpretation:</strong> Because when women are more focused
on pursuing higher levels of education and establishing careers, they
will start families at a later age. At that age, they might not be as
fertile to have many children. Moreover, the rising cost of living acts
as a disincentive for families to have more children because it is
financially unsustainable.</p>

<p><strong>Research support:</strong> A SG household survey study
conducted by NUS researchers found that later marriage was associated
with fewer children. Respondents also identified expected finances,
children’s education, childcare and housing costs as important
considerations in their fertility decisions. \[13\]</p>
::::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Insight 4: Policy and Recession Timing {.clean-slide}

::::: {.two-col .plot-wide}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.8
#| fig-height: 5.2
p_insight4
```

:::: side-note
::: kicker
Insight 4
:::

<h3>Policy and recession timing give context</h3>

<p>Some policy periods coincide with short-term changes, but no
sustained recovery appears.</p>

<p>Recession bands help show economic timing around policy windows.</p>

<p><strong>Interpretation:</strong> The policies introduced by the
government have limited effectiveness. Some of its effectiveness may be
compromised due to the enticing financial incentives during periods of
economic downturn.</p>

<p><strong>Research support:</strong> A study published in the Journal
of Social Policy identified a possible mismatch between some pronatalist
measures and the marriage and first-birth transitions most influential
to TFR. A nationally representative survey study published in the
Journal of Population Research also found that paternity leave, shared
parental leave and the Baby Bonus were perceived as supportive of
childbearing. \[11\]\[12\]</p>
::::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Limitations {.clean-slide}

::: kicker
Interpretation boundaries
:::

::: hr-accent
:::

<h4>What we can and cannot claim</h4>

:::::: limit-grid
::: limit-card
<h3>Association, not causation</h3>

<p>Policies, recessions and social indicators are used as timing
context. They do not prove a direct cause.</p>
:::

::: limit-card
<h3>Different measures</h3>

<p>ASFR, TFR, LFPR, education and age measures use different units, so
we avoid forcing them onto one scale unless clearly labelled.</p>
:::

::: limit-card
<h3>Period versus cohort</h3>

<p>TFR describes fertility in a year, while completed family size
describes older cohorts. Both are useful, but they answer different
questions.</p>
:::
::::::

## Conclusion {#conclusion .clean-slide .conclusion-slide}

::: kicker
Final takeaway
:::

::: hr-accent
:::

::: conclusion-big
Singapore's fertility decline is best read as a <span>linked structural change</span>, not a single drop caused by one policy, recession or demographic event.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="conclusion-points">
<div class="conclusion-point">
<h3>1. Young-age fertility weakened</h3>
<p>The final visual shows a clear fall in births among younger age groups, especially ages 15 to 24.</p>
</div>
<div class="conclusion-point">
<h3>2. Education and work patterns shifted</h3>
<p>Female education and LFPR rose over the same period, while marriage and first birth moved later.</p>
</div>
<div class="conclusion-point">
<h3>3. Smaller families became more common</h3>
<p>Completed family size shifted away from larger families, reinforcing the long-term fall in fertility.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

::: fragment
[Fertility declined not because of one turning point, but because multiple demographic, social and economic changes accumulated and reinforced one another over time. This suggests that addressing the issue will require equally multi-dimensional approaches, rather than isolated policy fixes.]{style="display:block; margin-top:28px; 
padding:14px 18px; 
background:rgba(0,0,0,0.03); 
border-left:5px solid #c0392b; 
font-size:1.12em; 
font-weight:500; 
line-height:1.6; 
color:#1f2d3d;"}
:::
